facts.statement: Inference is the process of drawing conclusions about a parameter from a sample. The two main areas of inferential statistics are estimation and testing of hypothesis. Estimating a parameter means using a statistic from the sample data (for example the sample mean) to say something about the population parameter (the population mean).

A point estimate is a single number used to estimate an unknown population parameter. It is either right or wrong, so on its own it does not show how wrong it might be. An interval estimate is a range of values used to estimate a parameter; it indicates the error by the extent of its range and by the probability of the true parameter lying within it. A point estimate is much more useful accompanied by an estimate of the error that might be involved.

A sample statistic used to estimate a population parameter is called an estimator (the sample mean for the population mean, the sample proportion for the population proportion, the sample range for the population range). A specific numerical value of an estimator observed in one sample is an estimate.

Four criteria of a good estimator: unbiased (the mean of its sampling distribution equals the parameter, so on average it is neither too high nor too low); efficient (it has the smaller standard error among competing statistics from samples of the same size, as when the standard error of the sample mean is 1.05 and that of the sample median is 1.6, so the mean is more efficient); consistent (as the sample size increases it becomes almost certain that the statistic is very close to the parameter); and sufficient (it uses so much of the information in the sample that no other estimator could extract more).
facts.locator: Printed pp. 136-137, Criteria of a Good Estimator

facts.statement: The sample mean x-bar is the point estimator of the population mean (it is unbiased, consistent and the most efficient, and its sampling distribution can be approximated by the normal distribution for a sufficiently large sample). In the courseware 35 cartons with total 3,570 syringes give x-bar = 102. The point estimator of the population variance is s^2 = Sum (x - x-bar)^2 / (n - 1); dividing by n gives an estimator with some bias. For five readings 4.33, 4.37, 4.36, 4.32 and 4.37 the courseware finds x-bar = 4.35 and s^2 = 0.0022 / 4 = 0.00055. The sample proportion p-bar is the point estimator of the population proportion p (unbiased, consistent, efficient and sufficient): 4 damaged cartons in 50 give p-bar = 0.08.

The standard error of the mean for an infinite population is sigma / sqrt(n); with sigma = 10 months and n = 200 batteries it is 10 / sqrt(200) = 0.707 month. The probability that a sample mean lies within plus or minus one, two and three standard errors of the population mean is 0.683, 0.955 and 0.997, so with a sample mean of 36 months the life lies between 35.293 and 36.707 months with 68.3 per cent confidence, between 34.586 and 37.414 months with 95.5 per cent and between 33.879 and 38.121 months with 99.7 per cent. A given interval either contains the population mean or does not, because the population mean is a fixed parameter; the confidence is that in 95.5 per cent of all samples the interval constructed contains it.

The probability associated with an interval estimate is its confidence level, and the range of the estimate is the confidence interval, with lower and upper confidence limits (LCL and UCL), written x-bar plus or minus z standard errors. About 90 per cent of the normal area lies within 1.64 standard errors, 95 per cent within 1.96 and 99 per cent within 2.58. The most used confidence levels are 90, 95 and 99 per cent, but any level may be used. A higher confidence level gives a wider and so less precise interval; a tighter interval has a lower confidence level. If many samples of the same size are drawn, about 95 per cent of the 95 per cent confidence intervals contain the population mean.

For a large sample (n > 30) the central limit theorem allows the normal distribution to be used even if the population is not normal. With known population standard deviation, the confidence limits for the mean are x-bar plus or minus z sigma / sqrt(n). Courseware example: n = 100 wiper blades, x-bar = 21 months, sigma = 6 months, standard error 0.6, 95 per cent confidence (z = 1.96), limits 21 - 1.18 = 19.82 and 21 + 1.18 = 22.18 months.

When the population standard deviation is unknown it is estimated by the sample standard deviation with divisor n - 1 (sigma-hat = s). If the population is finite and the sample is more than 5 per cent of it, the estimated standard error uses the finite population multiplier: sigma-hat of x-bar = (sigma-hat / sqrt(n)) x sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1)). Courseware example: N = 700 families, n = 50, x-bar = Rs 11,800, s = Rs 950 gives Rs 129.57, and the 90 per cent limits (z = 1.64) are Rs 11,587.50 and Rs 12,012.50.

For a proportion, the sampling distribution has mean p and standard error sqrt(pq / n); with p unknown it is estimated by sqrt(p-bar q-bar / n). The binomial can be approximated by the normal when n p and n q are both at least 5. Courseware example: n = 75 employees, p-bar = 0.4, estimated standard error sqrt(0.4 x 0.6 / 75) = 0.057, 99 per cent confidence (z = 2.58) limits 0.253 and 0.547.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 145-147, section 7.8 (the courseware rounds the standard error to 0.057 before computing the limits)

payload.title: Estimating: point, interval, estimator and estimate
payload.core_explanation_md:
We seldom know a population value (the average balance of **all** accounts, the share of **all** loans that will turn bad). We take a sample and **infer**.

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Estimator** | The sample statistic used (a formula or rule) | The sample mean |
| **Estimate** | The number that formula gives for one sample | Rs 18,400 |
| **Point estimate** | A single value | "The average balance is Rs 18,400" |
| **Interval estimate** | A range, with a probability attached | "Between Rs 17,900 and Rs 18,900, with 95 per cent confidence" |

A point estimate is either right or wrong, and it does not tell you how wrong. An interval estimate tells you both the likely **size of the error** (its width) and **how sure** you are (its probability).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Statistics has two main tools of inference: **estimation** (this unit) and **testing of hypotheses**. Estimation asks "what is the value?"; testing asks "is this claim about the value plausible?"

self_check.prompt_text: Is "the sample mean" an estimator or an estimate? And "Rs 18,400 from this sample"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The sample mean is an estimator (the rule); Rs 18,400 is an estimate (its value in one sample).

payload.title: Four marks of a good estimator
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Property | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Unbiased** | On average it hits the target: the mean of its sampling distribution equals the parameter, so it is not systematically too high or too low |
| **Efficient** | Among competing estimators it varies least from sample to sample, that is, it has the **smaller standard error** |
| **Consistent** | As the sample grows it gets almost certainly very close to the parameter |
| **Sufficient** | It uses all the information the sample holds about the parameter |

Example of efficiency: for samples of the same size the sample mean has a standard error of 1.05 and the sample median 1.6. The mean is the more efficient estimator of the population mean.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Consistency also tells you whether a bigger sample will help. If an estimator is not consistent, taking more observations wastes time and money.

self_check.prompt_text: Estimator A has a standard error of 2.0 and estimator B of 3.5, both unbiased. Which is more efficient, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A: with the same bias (none), the smaller standard error means less variation from sample to sample.

payload.title: Point estimators of the mean, variance and proportion
payload.core_explanation_md:
Three standard point estimators:

- **Mean**: the sample mean estimates the population mean.
- **Variance**: add the squared deviations from the sample mean and divide by **n - 1**, not n. Dividing by n gives an estimator that is biased (it tends to be too small), while dividing by n - 1 makes it **unbiased**.
- **Proportion**: the sample proportion p-bar = (number with the characteristic) / n estimates the population proportion.

The standard deviation estimate is the square root of the variance estimate.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Earlier, when describing a data set that was the whole population, the divisor was N. Here the data are a sample drawn to say something about a bigger population, so the divisor is n - 1.

assumptions: Simple random sample from the population.
n is at least 2 for a variance estimate.
common_errors: Dividing by n when estimating a population variance from a sample.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked.
Counting the population size in place of n.

self_check.prompt_text: Five readings have squared deviations adding to 90. What is the estimate of the population variance?

payload.title: Confidence levels and confidence intervals
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **confidence interval** is a sample mean plus or minus a multiple of the standard error:

**x-bar plus or minus z x (standard error)**, where z is chosen by how confident you want to be.

| Confidence level | z (standard errors either side) |
| --- | --- |
| 68.3 per cent | 1 |
| 90 per cent | 1.64 |
| 95 per cent | 1.96 |
| 95.5 per cent | 2 |
| 99 per cent | 2.58 |
| 99.7 per cent | 3 |

The ends are the **lower** and **upper confidence limits**.

**Trade-off.** More confidence needs a wider interval, and a wide interval is less precise. A 99 per cent interval is surer but fuzzier than a 90 per cent one.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A bank manager who wants a very precise estimate must accept less confidence, or take a bigger sample (which shrinks the standard error).

self_check.prompt_text: Which is wider, a 90 per cent or a 99 per cent interval from the same sample, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The 99 per cent interval: it uses 2.58 standard errors each side instead of 1.64, to be more sure of containing the parameter.

payload.title: Reading a confidence interval correctly
payload.core_explanation_md:
The population mean is a **fixed number**. It does not move; your interval does, from sample to sample.

So it is wrong to say "there is a 95 per cent chance that the mean lies in this interval". Say instead: **if we drew many samples and built an interval from each in the same way, about 95 per cent of those intervals would contain the true mean.** This particular interval either contains it or it does not; the 95 per cent describes the method.

A picture to hold: five intervals drawn from five samples; four catch the true mean, one misses.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In practice we have one sample and one interval, and we say we are 95 per cent confident because the method works 95 times in 100.

self_check.prompt_text: What does "95 per cent confident" describe: this one interval, or the method of building intervals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The method: about 95 per cent of intervals built this way contain the population mean.

payload.title: Interval estimate of a mean from a large sample (sigma known)
payload.core_explanation_md:
With a large sample (n above 30) the sample mean is approximately normal even if the population is not. So:

1. Find the standard error: sigma divided by the square root of n.
2. Pick z for the confidence level.
3. Add and subtract z standard errors from the sample mean.

Example shape: n = 100, mean 21 months, sigma 6 months. Standard error 0.6. For 95 per cent confidence the margin is 1.96 x 0.6 = 1.18, so the interval is 19.82 to 22.18 months.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The margin (z times the standard error) is the same on both sides. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error and so halves the margin.

assumptions: Infinite population, or a sample under 5 per cent of a finite one.
common_errors: Using sigma instead of sigma over the square root of n as the margin.
Choosing the wrong z for the confidence level.
Applying the formula to a small sample from a non-normal population.

self_check.prompt_text: Sample mean 50, sigma 12, n = 36, 95 per cent confidence. What are the limits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Standard error 2; margin 1.96 x 2 = 3.92; limits 46.08 and 53.92.

payload.title: When sigma is unknown, or the population is small
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two practical complications:

**sigma unknown.** Replace sigma by the sample standard deviation s, computed with divisor n - 1 (called sigma-hat).

**finite population.** If you sample more than 5 per cent of a finite population without replacement, shrink the standard error with the finite population multiplier:

estimated standard error = (sigma-hat over root n) x root of ((N - n) / (N - 1)).

Then build the interval as before.

Example: 700 families, sample 50, mean Rs 11,800, s = Rs 950. The sample is 7 per cent of the population, so the multiplier applies; the estimated standard error is Rs 129.57 and the 90 per cent limits are Rs 11,587.50 to Rs 12,012.50.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Skipping the multiplier when it is needed overstates the standard error and gives an interval that is wider than necessary.

variables.name: Sample standard deviation (divisor n - 1) used as the estimate of sigma

assumptions: Finite population, sampling without replacement, n/N above 0.05.
common_errors: Using divisor n for the sample standard deviation.
Applying the multiplier when the sample is under 5 per cent of the population.
Using the multiplier's square root incorrectly (N - n over N - 1, not N - n over N).

self_check.prompt_text: N = 100 and n = 25. Does the finite population multiplier apply, and what is its value?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes: 25 per cent is above 5 per cent. sqrt(75/99) = 0.8704.

payload.title: Interval estimate of a proportion from a large sample
payload.core_explanation_md:
Counting successes follows the binomial distribution, but for a large enough sample the **normal** distribution approximates it. The rule of thumb: both n times p and n times q must be **at least 5**.

Steps:

1. Sample proportion p-bar; q-bar = 1 - p-bar.
2. Estimated standard error = square root of (p-bar x q-bar / n).
3. Limits: p-bar plus or minus z standard errors.

Example: 75 employees, 40 per cent prefer their own retirement plan. Estimated standard error = sqrt(0.4 x 0.6 / 75), about 0.0566. At 99 per cent confidence (z = 2.58) the limits are about 0.254 and 0.546.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware rounds the standard error to 0.057 first, which gives limits 0.253 and 0.547. Rounding at the end gives 0.254 and 0.546; either way the story is the same.

assumptions: n p-bar and n q-bar both at least 5.
common_errors: Using the formula when n times p-bar or n times q-bar is below 5.
Forgetting to take the square root.
Expressing limits in per cent in one place and as a fraction in another.

self_check.prompt_text: n = 100 and p-bar = 0.4. What is the estimated standard error of the proportion?

payload.title: Estimating the mean and variance from six loan processing times
payload.core_explanation_md: Six randomly chosen loan applications took 4, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 12 days to process. Find the point estimates of the population mean and variance, and the variance you would get by wrongly dividing by n.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Mean estimate 8 days; variance estimate 8.4 days squared (standard deviation about 2.90 days); dividing by n would give 7.0, too small on average

self_check.prompt_text: Why is 8.4 preferred over 7.0 as an estimate of the population variance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Dividing by n - 1 makes the estimator unbiased; dividing by n tends to underestimate the variance.

payload.title: Loan processing time: intervals at three confidence levels
payload.core_explanation_md: For 64 loan applications the mean processing time is 18 days. The population standard deviation is known to be 4 days. Build intervals with confidence levels 68.3, 90, 95 and 99 per cent.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Intervals (days): 68.3 per cent 17.5 to 18.5; 90 per cent 17.18 to 18.82; 95 per cent 17.02 to 18.98; 99 per cent 16.71 to 19.29. More confidence, wider interval

self_check.prompt_text: What would you change to get a narrower 95 per cent interval?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Increase the sample size: the standard error (and so the margin) shrinks as n grows.

payload.title: Average balance when the population is small and sigma unknown
payload.core_explanation_md: A bank has 800 accounts of a certain type. A simple random sample of 100 (without replacement) has mean balance Rs 24,000 and sample standard deviation Rs 3,000. Estimate the mean balance of all 800 accounts with 90 per cent confidence.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: With 90 per cent confidence the mean balance of all 800 accounts lies between Rs 23539.49 and Rs 24460.51

self_check.prompt_text: What would the standard error be if the multiplier were wrongly omitted?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 300, which overstates it and widens the interval.

payload.title: Share of problem loans from a sample of 200
payload.core_explanation_md: In a random sample of 200 loans, 18 are non-performing. Estimate the proportion of non-performing loans in the whole portfolio with 95 per cent confidence.

worked_steps.description: Check the normal approximation: n p-bar and n q-bar.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: With 95 per cent confidence the portfolio's non-performing share lies between 5.03 and 12.97 per cent

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a sample of 200 enough for the normal approximation here?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both n p-bar = 18 and n q-bar = 182 exceed 5, which is the rule of thumb.

payload.title: How the margin responds to the sample size
payload.core_explanation_md: The population standard deviation is 12 and the confidence level is 95 per cent (z = 1.96). Compare the margin of error for samples of 36, 144 and 576.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Margins 3.92, 1.96 and 0.98: quadrupling the sample size halves the margin of error

self_check.prompt_text: To cut the margin to one-third, by what factor must n rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nine times, because the standard error varies with 1 divided by the square root of n.

items.title: Four marks of a good estimator
items.core_explanation_md:
| Property | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Unbiased** | On average it hits the target: the mean of its sampling distribution equals the parameter, so it is not systematically too high or too low |
| **Efficient** | Among competing estimators it varies least from sample to sample, that is, it has the **smaller standard error** |
| **Consistent** | As the sample grows it gets almost certainly very close to the parameter |
| **Sufficient** | It uses all the information the sample holds about the parameter |

Example of efficiency: for samples of the same size the sample mean has a standard error of 1.05 and the sample median 1.6. The mean is the more efficient estimator of the population mean.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Consistency also tells you whether a bigger sample will help. If an estimator is not consistent, taking more observations wastes time and money.

self_check.prompt_text: Estimator A has a standard error of 2.0 and estimator B of 3.5, both unbiased. Which is more efficient, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A: with the same bias (none), the smaller standard error means less variation from sample to sample.

items.title: Point estimators of the mean, variance and proportion
items.core_explanation_md:
Three standard point estimators:

- **Mean**: the sample mean estimates the population mean.
- **Variance**: add the squared deviations from the sample mean and divide by **n - 1**, not n. Dividing by n gives an estimator that is biased (it tends to be too small), while dividing by n - 1 makes it **unbiased**.
- **Proportion**: the sample proportion p-bar = (number with the characteristic) / n estimates the population proportion.

The standard deviation estimate is the square root of the variance estimate.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Earlier, when describing a data set that was the whole population, the divisor was N. Here the data are a sample drawn to say something about a bigger population, so the divisor is n - 1.

assumptions: Simple random sample from the population.
n is at least 2 for a variance estimate.
common_errors: Dividing by n when estimating a population variance from a sample.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked.
Counting the population size in place of n.

self_check.prompt_text: Five readings have squared deviations adding to 90. What is the estimate of the population variance?

items.title: Confidence levels and confidence intervals
items.core_explanation_md:
A **confidence interval** is a sample mean plus or minus a multiple of the standard error:

**x-bar plus or minus z x (standard error)**, where z is chosen by how confident you want to be.

| Confidence level | z (standard errors either side) |
| --- | --- |
| 68.3 per cent | 1 |
| 90 per cent | 1.64 |
| 95 per cent | 1.96 |
| 95.5 per cent | 2 |
| 99 per cent | 2.58 |
| 99.7 per cent | 3 |

The ends are the **lower** and **upper confidence limits**.

**Trade-off.** More confidence needs a wider interval, and a wide interval is less precise. A 99 per cent interval is surer but fuzzier than a 90 per cent one.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bank manager who wants a very precise estimate must accept less confidence, or take a bigger sample (which shrinks the standard error).

self_check.prompt_text: Which is wider, a 90 per cent or a 99 per cent interval from the same sample, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The 99 per cent interval: it uses 2.58 standard errors each side instead of 1.64, to be more sure of containing the parameter.

items.title: Reading a confidence interval correctly
items.core_explanation_md:
The population mean is a **fixed number**. It does not move; your interval does, from sample to sample.

So it is wrong to say "there is a 95 per cent chance that the mean lies in this interval". Say instead: **if we drew many samples and built an interval from each in the same way, about 95 per cent of those intervals would contain the true mean.** This particular interval either contains it or it does not; the 95 per cent describes the method.

A picture to hold: five intervals drawn from five samples; four catch the true mean, one misses.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In practice we have one sample and one interval, and we say we are 95 per cent confident because the method works 95 times in 100.

self_check.prompt_text: What does "95 per cent confident" describe: this one interval, or the method of building intervals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The method: about 95 per cent of intervals built this way contain the population mean.

items.title: Interval estimate of a mean from a large sample (sigma known)
items.core_explanation_md:
With a large sample (n above 30) the sample mean is approximately normal even if the population is not. So:

1. Find the standard error: sigma divided by the square root of n.
2. Pick z for the confidence level.
3. Add and subtract z standard errors from the sample mean.

Example shape: n = 100, mean 21 months, sigma 6 months. Standard error 0.6. For 95 per cent confidence the margin is 1.96 x 0.6 = 1.18, so the interval is 19.82 to 22.18 months.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The margin (z times the standard error) is the same on both sides. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error and so halves the margin.

assumptions: Infinite population, or a sample under 5 per cent of a finite one.
common_errors: Using sigma instead of sigma over the square root of n as the margin.
Choosing the wrong z for the confidence level.
Applying the formula to a small sample from a non-normal population.

self_check.prompt_text: Sample mean 50, sigma 12, n = 36, 95 per cent confidence. What are the limits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Standard error 2; margin 1.96 x 2 = 3.92; limits 46.08 and 53.92.

items.title: When sigma is unknown, or the population is small
items.core_explanation_md:
Two practical complications:

**sigma unknown.** Replace sigma by the sample standard deviation s, computed with divisor n - 1 (called sigma-hat).

**finite population.** If you sample more than 5 per cent of a finite population without replacement, shrink the standard error with the finite population multiplier:

estimated standard error = (sigma-hat over root n) x root of ((N - n) / (N - 1)).

Then build the interval as before.

Example: 700 families, sample 50, mean Rs 11,800, s = Rs 950. The sample is 7 per cent of the population, so the multiplier applies; the estimated standard error is Rs 129.57 and the 90 per cent limits are Rs 11,587.50 to Rs 12,012.50.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Skipping the multiplier when it is needed overstates the standard error and gives an interval that is wider than necessary.

variables.name: Sample standard deviation (divisor n - 1) used as the estimate of sigma

assumptions: Finite population, sampling without replacement, n/N above 0.05.
common_errors: Using divisor n for the sample standard deviation.
Applying the multiplier when the sample is under 5 per cent of the population.
Using the multiplier's square root incorrectly (N - n over N - 1, not N - n over N).

self_check.prompt_text: N = 100 and n = 25. Does the finite population multiplier apply, and what is its value?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes: 25 per cent is above 5 per cent. sqrt(75/99) = 0.8704.

items.title: Interval estimate of a proportion from a large sample
items.core_explanation_md:
Counting successes follows the binomial distribution, but for a large enough sample the **normal** distribution approximates it. The rule of thumb: both n times p and n times q must be **at least 5**.

Steps:

1. Sample proportion p-bar; q-bar = 1 - p-bar.
2. Estimated standard error = square root of (p-bar x q-bar / n).
3. Limits: p-bar plus or minus z standard errors.

Example: 75 employees, 40 per cent prefer their own retirement plan. Estimated standard error = sqrt(0.4 x 0.6 / 75), about 0.0566. At 99 per cent confidence (z = 2.58) the limits are about 0.254 and 0.546.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware rounds the standard error to 0.057 first, which gives limits 0.253 and 0.547. Rounding at the end gives 0.254 and 0.546; either way the story is the same.

assumptions: n p-bar and n q-bar both at least 5.
common_errors: Using the formula when n times p-bar or n times q-bar is below 5.
Forgetting to take the square root.
Expressing limits in per cent in one place and as a fraction in another.

self_check.prompt_text: n = 100 and p-bar = 0.4. What is the estimated standard error of the proportion?
